clinicalPearls: Pituitary adenomas are benign monoclonal neoplasms arising from one of the five anterior pituitary cell types; the secreted hormone (PRL, GH, ACTH, TSH, or LH/FSH) determines the clinical syndrome. About one-third are clinically nonfunctioning, most of these originating from gonadotrope or null cells (p.3003-3004).

Hormone output does not reliably track tumor size: small secretory microadenomas can be highly symptomatic, whereas large adenomas producing little hormone may stay clinically silent until mass effects appear (p.3003).

Suprasellar extension classically compresses the optic chiasm to produce bitemporal hemianopia, often worse superiorly, because crossing nasal ganglion-cell fibers in the ventral chiasm are most vulnerable; loss of red color perception can be an early sign (p.2998-2999).

The 'stalk section' phenomenon: any sellar mass that compresses the pituitary stalk and portal vessels causes early hyperprolactinemia (typically 30-100 ug/L) with later loss of other anterior pituitary hormones, even when the mass itself is not a prolactinoma (p.2998-2999).

Hyperprolactinemia is the most common pituitary hypersecretion syndrome; PRL levels above 200 ug/L almost always indicate a prolactin-secreting adenoma, while milder elevations are more often drug-induced, stalk-related, or due to hypothyroidism or renal failure (p.3004-3005).

Microprolactinomas show a marked female predominance (~20:1) and present early with amenorrhea/galactorrhea/infertility, whereas macroprolactinomas have a near 1:1 sex ratio and men tend to present later with larger, invasive tumors and mass effects (p.3005-3006).

Acromegaly is typically indolent and may go undiagnosed for a decade or more; acral and soft-tissue overgrowth (frontal bossing, prognathism, enlarged hands/feet, coarse features) plus visceromegaly are characteristic, and GH excess before epiphyseal closure causes gigantism (p.3008-3009).

Random single GH measurement is not diagnostic for acromegaly because of GH pulsatility; an age- and sex-matched IGF-1 is the screening test, and diagnosis is confirmed by failure of GH to suppress below threshold after an oral glucose load (p.3009).

Cushing's disease (corticotrope adenoma) accounts for ~70% of endogenous Cushing's syndrome, is 5-10 times more common in women, and the tumors are usually small microadenomas, about half undetectable on MRI (p.3010-3011).
Iatrogenic glucocorticoid use remains the most common overall cause of cushingoid features and must be excluded by history before pursuing an endogenous workup (p.3010).

ACTH-secreting adenomas retain partial suppressibility by high-dose glucocorticoids, distinguishing them from ectopic ACTH sources; inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH (central:peripheral ratio >2 basal, >3 post-CRH) has >95% sensitivity for localizing a pituitary source (p.3011-3012).

Nonfunctioning/gonadotrope adenomas are the most common adenoma type at presentation and are usually macroadenomas discovered through mass effect or as incidentalomas; mildly elevated PRL from stalk compression must not be mistaken for a true prolactinoma since these tumors do not shrink with dopamine agonists (p.3012-3013).

Most pituitary glands harbor an unsuspected microadenoma at autopsy (up to one-quarter), and imaging detects clinically inapparent lesions (incidentalomas) in at least 10% of people; small nonsecretory intrasellar lesions can be safely followed with serial MRI (p.2999, p.3003).
harrison.pathophysiology: Pituitary adenomas are benign, almost always monoclonal neoplasms derived from a single anterior pituitary cell lineage, implying acquisition of somatic mutation(s) conferring a growth advantage. Hormonally active tumors secrete autonomously with reduced responsiveness to physiologic feedback. Several molecular events are implicated: about 35% of GH-secreting tumors carry activating Gs-alpha mutations that lower GTPase activity, raise cyclic AMP, and drive somatotrope proliferation; growth factors (bFGF, EGFR signaling, the latter linked to USP8 mutation in some ACTH tumors), activated oncogenes (RAS, PTTG), loss of suppressors (e.g., MEG3), and loss of negative feedback (as in primary hypothyroidism/hypogonadism) also contribute. Hypothalamic hormones GHRH and CRH can additionally stimulate mitotic activity, so ectopic GHRH/CRH-producing chest or abdominal tumors can cause somatotrope or corticotrope hyperplasia. Familial settings include MEN 1 (MENIN, 11q13), MEN 4 (CDKN1B), Carney complex (PRKAR1A), McCune-Albright (mosaic Gs-alpha), and familial acromegaly (AIP). Clinical effects arise both from hormone hyper-/hyposecretion and from local mass effect: dorsal expansion lifts the optic chiasm, stalk compression disrupts dopaminergic inhibition of lactotropes (hyperprolactinemia) and portal hormone delivery, and lateral extension into the cavernous sinus impairs cranial nerves III, IV, VI and trigeminal branches.
additionalDifferentials: Craniopharyngioma (suprasellar cystic, often calcified, Rathke's pouch origin; BRAF V600E in papillary type)
Hypothalamic hamartoma or gangliocytoma (may secrete GnRH/GHRH/CRH)
Parasellar germ cell tumors (germinoma, dysgerminoma, teratoma, choriocarcinoma)
Pituitary metastases (esp. breast and lung; favor posterior pituitary)
Lymphoma, leukemia, plasmacytoma involving the sella
Macroprolactinemia (biologically inactive aggregated PRL causing falsely high PRL)
nonInfectiousMimics: Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia (antipsychotics esp. risperidone, metoclopramide, methyldopa, verapamil, estrogens, opiates, H2 blockers)
Chronic renal failure and cirrhosis (reduced PRL clearance)
Pregnancy, lactation, chest-wall stimulation, stress and sleep as physiologic PRL elevation
Polycystic ovarian syndrome (overlap with FSH/LH-secreting tumor causing ovarian hyperstimulation)
Iatrogenic/exogenous glucocorticoid excess mimicking Cushing's disease
Ectopic ACTH or ectopic CRH secretion mimicking Cushing's disease
Adrenal adenoma/carcinoma or adrenal hyperplasia as ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome
Ectopic GHRH (bronchial/abdominal carcinoid) or rare ectopic GH causing acromegaly
additionalInvestigations: Sagittal and coronal T1-weighted MRI before and after gadolinium (adenomas are hypodense on T1, brighter on T2); CT reserved for bony erosion or calcification
Formal perimetric visual field testing for any chiasm-impinging mass
Baseline pituitary hormonal screen: prolactin, IGF-1, 24-h urinary free cortisol and/or overnight 1-mg dexamethasone suppression, alpha-subunit/FSH/LH, and thyroid function tests
Acromegaly: IGF-1 (age/sex matched) and oral glucose tolerance test with GH at 0/30/60 min (failure to suppress confirms diagnosis)
Hyperprolactinemia: fasting morning PRL with sample dilution when very high (assay 'hook' artifact) and exclusion of macroprolactin
Cushing's disease: 24-h urinary free cortisol, overnight/low- and high-dose dexamethasone suppression, late-night salivary or midnight serum cortisol, basal ACTH, CRH stimulation
Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus ACTH sampling with CRH to localize an ACTH source when MRI is non-diagnostic
Gonadotropinoma/nonfunctioning: FSH, LH, free alpha-subunit, sex steroids; TRH stimulation may provoke atypical gonadotropin/subunit rise
TSH-secreting adenoma: free T4, free T3, TSH, alpha-subunit (inappropriately normal/high TSH with high free T4/T3)
Immunohistochemistry for hormones and cell-specific transcription factors on resected tissue for histologic confirmation
redFlags: Progressive visual field loss or new bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal compression)
Cranial nerve III/IV/VI palsy, diplopia, ptosis, or facial numbness indicating cavernous sinus invasion
Severe sudden headache with visual loss or ophthalmoplegia suggesting pituitary apoplexy (intratumoral hemorrhage/infarction)
Signs of raised intracranial pressure: headache, vomiting, papilledema, hydrocephalus
Arginine vasopressin deficiency (polyuria) as a presenting feature, which suggests posterior pituitary involvement or a non-adenomatous lesion such as metastasis or germ cell tumor
Rapid-onset hypercortisolism with hyperpigmentation, severe myopathy, and hypokalemic alkalosis suggesting an ectopic ACTH source
Features of acute adrenal insufficiency from coexisting hypopituitarism
harrison.prognosis: Pituitary tumors are overwhelmingly benign and slow growing; true carcinomas with extracranial metastases are exceedingly rare. Outcomes depend on tumor type and size and require lifelong follow-up. Prolactinomas respond well to dopamine agonists with normoprolactinemia and gonadal recovery in roughly 80% of microadenomas and tumor shrinkage in most macroadenomas; about 20% (especially men) are dopamine-resistant, and hyperprolactinemia may resolve spontaneously in up to 30% of hyperprolactinemic patients without a visible adenoma. Surgical PRL normalization reaches ~70% for microprolactinomas but only ~40% for macroadenomas, with substantial long-term recurrence (>50% for macroadenomas). In acromegaly, untreated GH excess roughly triples mortality and shortens survival by about 10 years, driven by cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and respiratory disease and increased colon cancer risk; transsphenoidal remission is ~70% for microadenomas and under 50% for macroadenomas. Cushing's disease has a microadenoma surgical remission of ~80% (<50% for macroadenomas), with ~5% biochemical recurrence and a postoperative period of ACTH deficiency. Untreated hypercortisolism carries excess mortality, chiefly cardiovascular, plus increased infection and suicide risk.
pitfalls: Assuming PRL suppression by a dopamine agonist proves a prolactinoma: stalk-compression hyperprolactinemia from a nonfunctioning mass also falls with dopamine agonists even though the mass does not shrink.
Very high prolactin levels (>1000 ug/L) may be reported falsely low due to assay 'hook' artifact unless the sample is diluted, leading to underestimation of macroprolactinoma.
Falsely elevated PRL from biologically inactive macroprolactin can prompt unnecessary evaluation.
Diagnosing acromegaly on a single random GH level is unreliable because of GH pulsatility; IGF-1 and a glucose-suppression test are required.
Attributing every small pituitary lesion to a secretory tumor: incidental microadenomas are very common, and ~50% of ACTH adenomas are MRI-occult, so imaging cannot reliably localize the ACTH source.
Overlap in basal ACTH levels between pituitary and ectopic ACTH sources means ACTH measurement alone cannot distinguish them; dynamic testing or petrosal sampling is needed.
Mistaking iatrogenic glucocorticoid excess for endogenous Cushing's syndrome.
Headache severity correlates poorly with adenoma size; a small intrasellar tumor can cause significant headache while a large tumor may not.
harrison.severityClassification: Pituitary adenomas are conventionally classified by size into microadenomas (<10 mm) and macroadenomas (>=10 mm, often locally invasive with parasellar extension), and by secretory phenotype into functioning (lactotrope/PRL, somatotrope/GH, corticotrope/ACTH, thyrotrope/TSH, gonadotrope/FSH-LH, or plurihormonal) versus clinically nonfunctioning (frequently gonadotrope or null-cell). Sellar mass severity is further graded by anatomic impact in Table 392-1 (compression of pituitary, optic chiasm, hypothalamus, cavernous sinus, frontal lobe, or brain), as larger/invasive tumors carry higher surgical risk and lower cure rates.
management: Dopamine agonists such as cabergoline or bromocriptine as first-line therapy for prolactinomas
Transsphenoidal surgery for non-functioning adenomas with mass effect, Cushing's disease, acromegaly and dopamine-agonist-resistant prolactinomas
Medical control of residual hormone excess with somatostatin ligands and pegvisomant for acromegaly and steroidogenesis inhibitors for hypercortisolism
Stereotactic or fractionated radiotherapy for residual or recurrent tumour after surgery
Replacement of any resulting anterior or posterior pituitary hormone deficiencies
Serial pituitary MRI, hormonal profiling and formal visual field testing for surveillance
Emergency management of pituitary apoplexy with stress-dose glucocorticoids and urgent surgical decompression where vision is threatened
Multidisciplinary neuroendocrine care involving neurosurgery, endocrinology and ophthalmology
